figures.alt: Photo of a bumblebee on a purple coneflower with pollen on its body.
figures.caption: Bees get nectar from flowers and move pollen from flower to flower.

figures.alt: Photo of three clear cups on a windowsill, each with a bean seedling: one tall and green, one thin and weak, one a dry brown stem.
figures.caption: An example of what bean cups can look like after two weeks: strong, weak, and dead.

figures.alt: Photo of a robin perched on a branch with a red berry in its beak.
figures.caption: Birds eat berries and carry the seeds to new places. The berry is food for the bird.

figures.alt: Photo of a forest floor with a deer, a squirrel on a branch, mushrooms and a beetle.
figures.caption: A forest has many kinds of living things. Count the kinds you can see.

figures.alt: Illustration of a grandfather in a sun hat and two children looking at a bumblebee on a purple coneflower in a meadow, one child pointing at the bee.
figures.caption: Bees visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen along, so plants can make seeds.

figures.alt: Grouped bar graph of bean height in paper clips. Sun and water: 4 on day 7, 9 on day 14. No sun, water: 4 and 7. Sun, no water: 1 and 1. No sun, no water: 1 and 1.
figures.caption: Example: bean heights in paper clips on day 7 and day 14. Sun + water grew most (9). No sun + water grew to 7 but was pale yellow and floppy. Without water, the beans stayed at 1.

figures.alt: Bar graph, Kinds of living things counted. Forest 6 kinds, Dune 3 kinds.
figures.caption: The forest picture set had 6 kinds of living things. The dune picture set had 3 kinds.
